analysis.one_liner: Bans states from making online sellers without in-state stores collect sales tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Supreme Court's then-existing rule (Quill v. North Dakota), a state could only require a retailer to collect its sales tax if that retailer had a physical presence in the state. This bill would write that rule into federal law and go further: a state could not even assess sales-type taxes on, or demand information from, a seller with no physical presence, and federal courts could block states that tried. The practical effect would be to keep the online-sales tax gap open permanently, at the cost of state revenue and the competitive position of local stores. The bill died in the House Judiciary Committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Online retailers selling into states where they have no stores, warehouses, or employees. They would never have to collect sales tax on those sales, keeping their prices up to several percentage points lower than local competitors who must collect.

how_it_helps.text: Bars states from imposing sales and use tax collection duties, assessments, or information-reporting demands on any person without a physical presence in the state during the quarter.

Sets narrow physical-presence tests: a store, warehouse, or property; employees soliciting orders in the state; on-site installation or repair staff; or an office with three or more employees — and carves out referral agreements, presences under 15 days a year, common-carrier delivery, and certain Internet advertising as not counting.
Defines marketplace providers, referrers, carriers, and credit-card or payment intermediaries as outside the definition of seller, so they could not be treated as the party that must collect.
Gives U.S. district courts original jurisdiction to enforce the ban, including injunctive relief against states.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, whose sales tax collections on remote sales would shrink, and their residents, who would face either service cuts or higher taxes elsewhere. In-state brick-and-mortar retailers also pay in lost competitiveness.

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip states of revenue from remote sales — money states typically fund schools, roads, and police with — forcing cuts or higher taxes on people who do pay.

It would lock in a two-tier system: local stores collect tax on every sale while online rivals selling into the same state collect nothing, handing the online seller a built-in price advantage on Main Street.
Consumers technically still owe 'use tax' on untaxed remote purchases, but few pay it, so the revenue quietly disappears rather than shifting to anyone.
It preempts state tax authority in an area states have historically governed, which even supporters of tax limits acknowledged as an unusually strong federal intrusion on state fiscal policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For remote sellers and their customers at checkout, the bill is a win: no tax line on the receipt. But the cost does not disappear — it moves to state budgets and to every local store competing against an untaxed online rival. Because purchasers still legally owe the tax, the bill mainly converts a public revenue stream into a private discount. An honest supporter would concede the bill trades state solvency and Main Street fairness for a narrow checkout convenience.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, and it sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner (R-WI) introduced the bill on July 14, 2016.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
On August 10, 2016, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law.
No further action was taken; the bill had zero cosponsors and died at the end of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online sellers, who kept the untaxed-remote-sale advantage, and state governments, which retained their existing authority over sales tax collection (later expanded after the Supreme Court's 2018 Wayfair decision) — better off than they would have been under this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online sellers; states kept their authority

for.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner (R-WI)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Panel to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it moved only as far as a subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or cosponsors exist to show a partisan pattern; a senior Republican sponsored it and no member of either party signed on.

industries.note: The bill would make permanent their exemption from collecting sales tax on out-of-state sales, converting tax their customers owe into a permanent price discount. The gain comes directly out of state budgets and local stores' competitiveness.
The bill would preserve the current-law price advantage of online competitors over local stores, since in-state stores must collect tax on every sale and online rivals would not.
States would lose the ability to assess sales-type taxes on remote sellers or demand information from them, shrinking a core revenue source for services residents use.

industries.industry: Marketplace platforms, referrers, and payment processors
industries.note: The bill defines these intermediaries out of the 'seller' category entirely, ensuring they could never be made the party that collects the tax — locking in their role as untaxed channels for remote commerce.
